2.text: It seems that the ideas of the American Eskimo are clearer about “masters”

3.text: living within material objects. Thus among the Central Eskimo, according to

4.text: Professor Boas,¹ large bowlders scattered over the country are considered to

5.text: have spirits of their own. Such a spirit is represented as a woman with a

6.text: single eye in the middle of her forehead. Others live in stones that roll down

7.text: the hill in spring. When, however, a stone like that is met by a native,

8.text: and is asked to become his supernatural assistant, it simply has to accompany

9.text: him, wobbling along because it has no legs.

10.text: The idea of bowlders being the habitation of spirits of human form is

11.text: foreign to the mind of the Chukchee.² The bowlders of their own country,

12.text: numbers of which are to be met with everywhere in the mountains, are considered

13.text: by the Chukchee as beings which were formerly alive, but were subsequently

14.text: turned into stone. They were the first attempts of the Creator to form living

15.text: beings, but they proved so clumsy in shape that he transformed them into

16.text: stone, and then created actual men and animals. Those bowlders are called

17.text: pêˊrkat (pl. of pêrkaˊpêr). Some of them represent petrified houses or tents:

20.text: tale a shaman wants to try a wrestling-match with a Bowlder-Man, and comes

21.text: very badly out of his stony embrace. In another tale a group of Bowlder-Men

22.text: become alive and talk among themselves. The difference between this view

23.text: and the Eskimo idea of “masters” in bowlders is very apparent.

27.text: OWNERS OR MASTERS. — Larger material unities, such as forests, rivers,

28.text: lakes, etc., have special “owners” (êtɪˊnvɪt, pl. of êˊtɪn), who are also called
28.resolved: ê = e+U+0302 (×2); ɪ = U+026A small-cap I (×2); ˊ = U+02CA word stress (×2)

29.text: “masters” (aunraˊlɪt, pl. of aunraˊlɪn, literally, “chief [in the] house”).

30.text: Various classes of animals and trees also have their “masters,” who live

31.text: in the forest with them. Each species of tree has a separate “master.” The

32.text: birch alone has none, and for that reason, men handle it without precaution,

33.text: as “their equal.” The latter conception is clearly connected with the yearly

34.text: expeditions of the Reindeer Chukchee into the woods to procure birch, of

35.text: which they make their sledges, the shafts of spears, etc. Each species of

36.text: wild animal — fox, wolf, reindeer — has a “master” of its own.³

37.text: The Chukchee often call all these “masters” simply “spirits” (keˊlet).

39.text: ² In a story of Alaskan Eskimo (Nelson, p. 465), a whale has a “master” living inside its body, and

40.text: controlling its motions. The whale is a female, and so is its “master,” a point of similarity between the two.

41.text: The idea of an animal having an “owner” spirit within its body, however, does not occur among the Chukchee.

42.text: ³ This latter conception has developed, perhaps, from the idea of the “master” of the forest, who owns

43.text: all game living within the limits of his dominions. Thus, according to the Russo-Yukaghir belief, the “master”

44.text: of the forest has absolute power over his animals. He may give them away as presents, lose them in card-

45.text: playing, make them gather in herds and depart from the country, etc. Compare p. 287.
